working_title: England's Forgotten Links Coast: A Practical Guide to Playing Golf in Cumbria
angle: Cumbria is routinely skipped by golfers heading north to Scotland or south to Lancashire, yet it quietly hosts some of the most compelling links golf in England. The post makes the case for a dedicated Cumbrian golf trip built around Silloth-on-Solway, Seascale, and Furness (Walney Island), with honest notes on the effort required to get there and why it rewards that effort.
research_notes:
- Silloth-on-Solway Golf Club: founded 1892 by the North British Railway Company, originally laid out by Davy Grant; Willie Park Jr. and Willie Fernie consulted on early layout; Dr Alister MacKenzie made some alterations pre-WWII (tight budget meant only a few proposals were used). Listed in the top 50 golf courses in Britain and Ireland. Sits on the Solway Firth in north-west Cumbria; views across the Firth to the Scottish Borders on one side, Lake District fells on the other. Traditional links with undulating fairways, firm fast greens, heather and gorse flanking fairways. Has hosted Regional Qualifying for The Open Championship, British Ladies Championship, English Amateur Championship, and in 2022 the Carris Trophy. Regularly described as one of the most remote of England's great courses, and as genuinely underpriced relative to quality.
- Seascale Golf Club: founded 1893, designed by Willie Campbell and George Lowe. Championship links, 6,450 yards, SSS 71. Included in the Rolex World's Top 1000 Golf Courses and rated in the top 100 courses in England by Top100GolfCourses. Situated on the west Cumbria coast with views of the Isle of Man and Scotland to the west, Lake District peaks to the east. Approximately one hour south of Silloth. The Sellafield plant is visible from some holes to the north but does not dominate the experience; westerly and southerly holes face open Irish Sea. Visitors welcome; buggy hire and practice ground available.
- Furness Golf Club (Old Links), Walney Island: founded 1872, the 3rd oldest links and 6th oldest golf club in England. Originally founded by Scottish migrant workers from Dundee as a 6-hole course on Biggar Bank, later expanded to 18 holes (6,363 yards, par 71). Accessed from Barrow-in-Furness via the Jubilee Bridge. Views of the Irish Sea and Lakeland hills from every hole. Features a notable par-3 10th that drops approximately 100ft from tee to pin. Visitors welcome every day. Self-described as probably the best-kept golfing secret in the north-west.
- Getting there: Cumbria's west coast is not on a main rail corridor; driving is the most practical option for a multi-course trip. Silloth is roughly 25 miles west of Carlisle. Seascale is served by the Cumbrian Coast railway line (Carlisle to Barrow). Walney Island is accessed from Barrow-in-Furness.
- Accommodation: range from luxury (e.g. resort hotels near Carlisle) to B&Bs in Silloth itself. The Cumbrian coastal route links courses well as a self-drive itinerary.
- The county has 30+ courses overall, including parkland options at Carlisle Golf Club (founded 1908, near M6 J43) and Penrith, giving non-links days as options for mixed-ability groups.
- Pricing: do NOT invent specific current green fees. Sources older than 2023 cite figures that may be out of date. Advise readers to check club websites directly.
- Key tone point: the remoteness is the point. These courses exist in relative anonymity largely because they are hard to reach, not because they are unworthy.
